A Probabilistic Approximate Logic for
Neuro-Symbolic Learning and Reasoning
Mark-Oliver Stehr ⇤, Minyoung Kim, Carolyn L. Talcott
SRI International, 333 Ravenswood Ave., Menlo Park, CA 94025
Abstract
As witnessed by recent advances in deep learning technologies, neural network
models of very high complexity have been successfully applied in many data-rich
domains. Challenges remain, however, if the amount of training data is severely
limited, which is often the case due to the cost of acquiring such data or due to
interest in systems that are constantly evolving thereby imposing natural limits
on how much data can be collected. The core hypothesis explored in this paper
is that data (to some degree) can be substituted by domain knowledge, not only
addressing the limited data problem but also o ↵ering potential improvements
in data-rich settings. For the representation of suitable domain theories, we
propose Probabilistic Approximate Logic (PALO) to deal with the natural un-
certainty associated with such representations and also to serve as a foundation
for a new class of neuro-symbolic architectures, in which both neural and sym-
bolic computations can be peacefully and synergistically integrated. Utilizing
TensorFlow and Maude as neural and symbolic frameworks, respectively, we
discuss our prototypical implementation of PALO in what we call the Logical
Imagination Engine (LIME). By means of a small toy example, we convey a
glimpse of its capabilities, but we also brieﬂy discuss some real-world applica-
tions and how it may serve as a prototypical framework to explore a broader
range of neuro-symbolic strategies in the future.
Keywords: Neuro-Symbolic Architecture, First-Order Logic, Probabilistic
Logic, Machine Learning, Neural Networks

In this paper, we introduce Probabilistic Approximate Logic (PALO) as a
logic based on the notion of mean approximate probability to overcome concep-
tual and computational di �culties inherent to strictly probabilistic logics. The
logic is approximate in several dimensions. Logical independence assumptions
are used to obtain approximate probabilities, but by averaging over many in-
stances of formulas a useful estimate of mean probability with known conﬁdence
can usually be obtained. To enable e �cient computational inference, the logic
has a continuous semantics that reﬂects only a subset of the structural properties
of classical logic, but this imprecision can be partly compensated by richer the-
ories obtained by classical inference or other means. Computational inference,
which refers to the construction of models and validation of logical properties, is
based on Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) and Markov Chain Monte Carlo
(MCMC) techniques and hence another dimension where approximations are
involved. The propositional core of PALO is based on ingredients from Hajek’s
Product logic,  Lukasiewicz logic, and G¨ odel logic, but a non-standard seman-
tics of quantiﬁers and theories is the key to a probabilistic interpretation and a
practical implementation giving rise to a ﬁrst-order stochastic logic. A notion
of imagination will be introduced as Bayesian inference in a generalized model
space that allows both logical theories and models to morph simultaneously and
synergistically in the learning process.

2. Related Work
Building on the work of Bacchus [2], Halpern [26] considered two classical
probabilistic ﬁrst-order logics and their combination. The ﬁrst logic assumes
that the domain of each variable constitutes a probability distribution, while
the second uses a semantics where formulas are interpreted w.r.t. a set of
worlds which is equipped with a probability distribution. PALO is not a classi-
cal logic but rather a soft logic with a continuous interpretation of propositions
as real numbers in the interval [0 , 1]. Domains are not equipped with proba-
bility distributions, but propositional formulas are interpreted as approximate
probabilities. Such probabilities are lifted to quantiﬁed formulas by averaging
to compensate for their approximate nature. Probabilities are further lifted to
models of theories in a way that compensates for the natural uncertainty in
the weight/relevance of the axioms. This last point is essential because as a
substructural logic a soft logic is necessarily incomplete w.r.t. to a classical
semantics, which is more intuitive for the user to reason with, and hence an im-
portant reference inﬂuencing the design of PALO and its use. Like in traditional
ﬁrst-order logic, PALO theories are typically interpreted by classes of models
(which may be called worlds), but to avoid any misconceptions we should men-
tion that these models are not equipped with any additional structure (e.g., an
accessibility relation) as in modal or temporal logics.
The idea of viewing probabilities as generalized truth values goes back to
Reichenbach [48] but has remained unsatisfactory due to the non-extensional
(in other words, non-truth-functional or non-denotational) nature of this inter-
pretation. Generally, the probability p(� ^  ) can not be deﬁned as a function
of p(�) and p( ), and assumptions need to be made to achieve a strict corre-
spondence to a meaningful probability. Our approach is conceptually related to
a solution proposed by Gaines [18]. He deﬁnes what he calls a Standard Uncer-
tainty Logic (SUL) that by simple axiomatic extensions yields either Stochastic
Logic or Fuzzy Logic. Both logics can be equipped with a population semantics
(not necessarily limited to human individuals), where in case of the Stochastic
Logic p(�^ ) can be interpreted as a product p(�)p( ) with a suitable indepen-
dence assumption that can be realized ”externally” by ”choosing a number of
di↵erent individuals at random to answer each question involved in evaluating a
compound”. Gaines considered only propositional logic, but in the more general
ﬁrst-order setting of PALO we also need to deﬁne the semantics of quantiﬁers,
which helps us to realize his idea in a quite natural fashion. Another di ↵erence
to Gaines’ work is that as a soft logic PALO does not satisfy the strict absorp-
tion (and hence idempotence) axioms of SUL and the additional distributivity
and excluded middle axiom of Stochastic Logic (which is still a classical logic).
It does so however with increasing precision when approaching the classical limit
case where interpretations are constrained to {0, 1}.
It is noteworthy that our approach of combining selected operators from Ha-
jek’s Product logic,  Lukasiewicz logic, and G¨ odel logic in a non-standard fashion
needs to be di ↵erentiated from work in the area of fuzzy logics, which is not
aiming at a probabilistic interpretation but an orthogonal notion of truthiness

Incidence Calculus [9] is another approach to overcome the fact that a proba-

semantics that interprets each formula as the set of assignments for which it
holds so that conjunction becomes a simple intersection. Although this is an
elegant solution, with our mean probability semantics that includes lower and
upper bounds, it turns out that the bounds are su �ciently tight so that replac-

the data-rich applications we are targeting. Two other practical di �culties with
an exact probabilistic semantics are that dependencies between subformulas re-
ferring to external data are often unknown and even if all known dependencies
would be taken into account it would lead to an unacceptably high computa-
tional complexity in the context of model generation and learning.

Quite di ↵erent from all the approaches listed above, one objective of PALO
is to provide a semantic framework in which neural and symbolic computations
can coexist and synergistically interact. A recent classiﬁcation of neuro-symbolic
approaches related to logics can be found in [4] and nicely illustrates the diver-

quite diverse set of approaches (including, for example, agent-based systems) as
summarized in the excellent survey [6].
To our knowledge there are only a few existing frameworks (developed in
the context of logic programming) that genuinely integrate symbolic and neural
(also called subsymbolic) computations. With the notion of a Neural Theorem
Prover [51] introduces a di ↵erentiable framework for theorem proving inspired
by Prolog’s backward chaining algorithm. In a nutshell, the concept of variable
binding is treated symbolically but symbols are compared using their subsym-
bolic vector representations (which can be learned), essentially implementing a
form of soft uniﬁcation. An attractive feature of this approach is that multi-hop
reasoning can be supported in a fully di ↵erentiable way. As a key application
of end-to-end di ↵erentiability, a form of Neural Inductive Logic Programming
is supported. Note that the learning is focussed on the logic program (i.e., on
the rules) unlike PALO which is more concerned with learning logical models
(although there are also logical weights that can be learned). A quite di ↵erent
approach is taken in DeepProbLog [40], which integrates neural networks into
a probabilistic logic framework, and in fact can be regarded as an extension of
ProbLog [14]. As a logic programming framework it comes with a closed-world
semantics (Herbrand interpretation) which di ↵erentiates it from the open-world
semantics of PALO, which is not tied to the syntactic realm. The key idea is
that neural networks can be used to realize certain (annotated) disjunctions in
the logic program by using them as probabilistic classiﬁers (e ↵ectively deciding
which choice to take). An interesting feature of DeepProbLog is its capability
to perform program induction, where holes in given programs can be ﬁlled by
neural networks based on input/output samples for the whole program. On the
other hand, it is noteworthy the the probabilities associated with rules (syntactic
level) in probabilistic logic programs are not directly related to the (approxi-
mate) probabilities arising from the interpretation of formulas in PALO, which
depend on the logical model under consideration and on the data (semantic
level). It is quite interesting to see that according to [4], LTNs and Deep-
ProbLog achieve similar performance on a toy example utilizing the MNIST
handwritten digits dataset, in spite of being completely di ↵erent approaches
(e.g., no symbolic computations are taking place in LTNs).

3. Syntax and Semantics of P ALO
PALO is an evolving language directly driven by applications. For clarity, we
focus on the current design for the core language and semantics of PALO in this
section. The full semantics of PALO combines a mean probability interpretation
of formulas with upper and lower bounds and will be introduced in several
stages. In addition, two types of classical semantics with di ↵erent degrees of
abstraction will be deﬁned to highlight, quantify, and take advantage of the
connection to classical logic, and hence serve as a formal justiﬁcation of the
larger neuro-symbolic framework that we are proposing and initially exploring
in this paper. A number of practically important extensions will be discussed
in Section 5, and for most parts, our deﬁnitions should be su �ciently general
to accommodate these extensions with minor modiﬁcations.

4.3. Other Applications of PALO/LIME
For the purpose of this paper, the objective of our toy example was to illus-
trate the use of PALO/LIME in a simple end-to-end machine learning workﬂow.
In previous work, that we brieﬂy summarize below, we applied PALO/LIME to
more complex theories, more precisely di ↵erent theories of causal relations (in
43

a partial order sense that also plays an important role in the foundations of
distributed systems). In fact, our original motivation to develop PALO came
from the biological domain, speciﬁcally the DARPA Rapid Threat Assessment
(RTA) program, where in a multi-disciplinary team we developed data analysis
and machine-learning techniques to support biologists in understanding the so-
called Mechanism of Action (MOA) that is triggered when an (unknown) drug
or toxic substance hits a human cell. From relatively short windows of time
after the event in question (usually 48 hours) these algorithms generate graphs
representing networks of potential causality (as concise and competing explana-
tions of the observed time series). The inputs for our algorithms are time series
of typically high-dimensional measurements, e.g., transcriptomics (we used gene
expression microarray data of ⇠18K of protein-coding genes), proteomics, and
metabolomics data. We have also developed algorithms for anomaly detection
that highlight certain nodes in such graphs as potentially impacted and allow
the biologist to narrow down the Mechanism of Action.
The algorithms we developed in DARPA RTA [67, 66, 61] use a variety of
models ranging from Gaussian Processes (on non-linear time scales) to various
types of neural networks (e.g., convolutional autoencoders, deep & wide neural
networks, Siamese neural networks, and Generative Adversarial Networks) to
detect anomalies, potential causality, and to synthesize corresponding graphs
from experimental data. Usually the set of graphs can be further reduced to the
most promising candidates by subject matter expertise (in this case involving
our biologists). While our algorithms often yielded interpretable results, a com-
mon problem was that domain knowledge is either represented implicitly or not
at all. Intuitively, biological causal networks have structural properties that if
properly represented should improve the learned models, which led us to explore
the use of LTNs (the early 2018 version) and further evolve it into PALO to deal
with approximate probabilistic knowledge [62]. Unlike our toy example in this
paper, which is purely functional/equational, the domain theory for RTA was
deﬁned by multiple interrelated relations and uses all the operators that PALO
o↵ers. This includes the existential quantiﬁer which posed some interesting
computational challenges due to its non-continuous nature that we addressed
using a curriculum-learning approach (see experimental features of LIME dis-
cussed in Section 4). Focussing on the transcriptomics data, the inputs to
PALO/LIME are the set of genes (utilizing a dimensionality-reduced represen-
tation of their Gaussian Processes) and high-probability causality/independence
relations established by our causality detectors. The synthesized models contain
probabilistic relations that can be depicted as directed causal graphs, typically
using suitable probabilistic cuto ↵s to focus on high probability subgraphs which
can then be further explored and interpreted by our biologists. The advantage
of this approach is that local causality detectors can be combined with global
knowledge (or hypotheses) about the causal network structure and hence can
potentially lead to more realistic models. In other words, it facilitates the work
of biologists by allowing them to focus on a smaller set of candidate models
because implausible models have more likely been ﬁltered out.
To understand if our approach may have applicability beyond biological sys-

tems, we have in a preliminary study applied it to global ﬁnancial markets,
another type of a complex networked cyber-physical system that comes with
additional challenges (e.g., the impossibility to conduct reproducible experi-
ments). As a starting point, we used ﬁnancial time series data around events
that can cause signiﬁcant perturbations of the system giving us a chance to
extract potential causality graphs. While the approach is more general, in our
case study, we focussed on FOMC 47 announcements by the Federal Reserve,
which in a sense can be seen as determining the type and the dose of a drug
given to the markets. Utilizing a variation of the theory of causal relations
developed for DARPA RTA, we tested PALO/LIME on various ﬁnancial instru-
ments (⇠3000 equities, ⇠1500 funds, ⇠100 currency pairs, and ⇠150 futures) for
FOMC events in 2017 and 2018. The synthesized graphs, which can be regarded
as candidates for a Mechanism of Action of the FOMC operations, turned out
to be quite plausible and might be potentially eye-opening for market partici-
pants and regulators. Being based on neural networks, our approach can detect
a broader class of (non-linear) causal relations between ﬁnancial instruments
than traditional cross-correlation-based approaches. However, what might be
more interesting for ﬁnancial market experts is the potential to identify hidden
relationships (possibly risks) that are invisible by looking at time series data
alone but only emerge by incorporating the global causal structure of the graph
(which is usually beyond human comprehension due to its size).
5. Extensions of the Core Logic and its Engine
To evolve PALO into a practical general-purpose language for machine learn-
ing applications a lot of work remains to be done. In the following, we list, in
our view, the most important directions for future extensions and generaliza-
tions ranked by increasing di �culty and level of e ↵ort. Many of these directions
will be guided by our long-standing experience with Maude in many di ↵erent
application domains and by the question of how features of Maude could be
best leveraged in the machine learning domain.
Built-ins, Mixﬁx Syntax, Overloading, Subsorts, and Richer Models. Most ap-
plications have special needs for arithmetic and logical 48 operators. In our
prototype, such operators could be deﬁned in TensorFlow/Python by means of
semantic attachments. Also, note that our tensor abstractions provide a con-
venient way to also introduce new higher-order operators like min and max
operators or corresponding soft versions for arbitrary terms. From a practical
point of view, it will be convenient to organize such built-ins in theory libraries
very much like the built-in operators of Maude. Ideally, such libraries can evolve
without modifying the PALO syntax. One natural solution is to support the

to improve the PALO core logic by adding subsort and membership assertions

coincides with the standard semantics [8] in the classical limit case. 49
On the semantic side, a more general notion of semantic attachment (with a
ﬂexible interpretation that depends on new model parameters) has already been
introduced by associating predicate and function symbols with other learnable
families of semantic functions that can be represented as TensorFlow graphs
with variables (e.g., deep neural networks as black-box components). The ex-
pressiveness of PALO could be further improved by introducing suitable types
for each new family. We also anticipate that the set of built-in learnable families
will be further extended as our experience with applications grows, again ideally
through the use of theory libraries. For example, we plan to introduce learnable
piecewise linear functions as a natural generalization of linear functions. Other
classes of functions of practical interest are multivariate polynomials and sub-
classes, e.g., the class of functions used in factorization machines [49]. Richer
interpretations for predicates are also conceivable, for example, their represen-
tation as deep Sum-Product Networks [44]. Besides, more domain/application-
speciﬁc libraries should be developed including parameterized families of com-
mon neural network architectures such as deep convolutional networks. To re-
duce complexity and improve scalability, learning could proceed hierarchically,
or according to more ﬂexible user-deﬁned strategies, which is connected to the
topic of compositionality and modularity (see below).
Equational Logic and Structural Symmetries. An important concept that we
added to PALO in this paper is approximate equality. The power of equality
is witnessed by many of the traditional symbolic logical systems. For example,
in Maude [64] which is based on membership equational logic [8], a conditional
equational logic with sorts, the focus on equality leads to very intuitive exe-
cutable speciﬁcations and supports its use as a logical and semantic framework
for other formalisms [42]. Clearly, without equality the use of functions is some-
what limited. Interestingly, there is not a single concept of equality once we
accept that it must be approximate. We currently support built-in notions of
equality based on L1 or L2 norm or more application-specify equality predicates
via semantic attachments. 50
However, our symmetric notion of equality is only one possibility, and there
is also an alternative view suggested by Maude’s rewriting logic [43], which itself

was inspired by linear logic and can be regarded as an extreme substructural

interpretation of equality in terms of rewriting with many interesting logical and
semantic framework applications such as in the representation of deductive or
concurrent systems. Approximating this notion in PALO/LIME would lead to
a more reﬁned notion of equality. We envision that like in Maude both notions
should be able to peacefully coexist.
There is also a third notion of structural equality in Maude, that is based
on built-in equational theories. All computations in Maude take place modulo
such equational theories, thereby elevating the level of computational abstrac-
tion. Such structural equations can also be a powerful feature as they may allow
us to express symmetries that can be e �ciently realized by submodules such as
deep symmetry networks [19]. Structural equality can be further generalized to
cover (logical) structural equivalence. For example, it is conceivable that cer-
tain common properties of predicates (e.g., reﬂexivity, irreﬂexivity, symmetry,
asymmetry, transitivity) can be enforced structurally by suitable classes of neu-
ral networks (the Siamese networks used in [61] are only one example) resulting
in increased learning and inference e �ciency. This naturally leads to the topic
of modularity of logical theories and their corresponding neural networks.
Modularity and Composability of Theories. Modules and theories (optionally
parameterized) are a key feature of the Maude semantics that allows it to scale
to larger applications. To cover this topic it is useful to adopt a dual view of
logic as a means of knowledge representation as well as an architectural descrip-
tion language. It suggests that the natural modular structure of the domain
theory (including any inferred domain knowledge) should lead to a correspond-
ing modular structure of the neural network that is synthesized from it. The
modular structure of the neural network (which can be made explicit using con-
structs such as hierarchical scoping in TensorFlow [1]) can then be exploited
for compositional training strategies. For example, a basic strategy of con-
current training simply trains components independently and composes them
afterward. In sequential training, components are trained layerwise, by training
and freezing the models of lower layers before higher layers are trained. More
ﬂexible strategies perform pretraining [15] of basic components before they are
composed and then continue the training process in a larger context without
freezing the pretrained models, thus allowing the smaller modules to adapt to
the bigger context. Interestingly, there is a counterpart to the common tech-
nique of freezing neural network models in the logical world of Maude, where the
module system allows theories to be included in other theories with a seman-
tic protection constraint, e ↵ectively expressing that semantics of the included
theory should not be a ↵ected by the including theory. This suggests that it
might be feasible to develop a declarative approach to module composition that
generalizes and uniﬁes traditional techniques in algebraic speciﬁcations, logics
and machine learning.
Conventional approaches to deep learning do not have access to an explicit
representation of the domain theory , which is a big disadvantage that must be
47

compensated by manual, error-prone engineering. Thanks to our logical frame-
work, we can exploit the structure of the theory to automatically synthesize the
proper architecture of the neural network and corresponding training strategies
tailored to the network structure, the type of problem, and the type of data.
Another practical beneﬁt of our envisioned modular approach is the ability to
integrate existing well-tested black-box components (i.e., modules that are not
necessarily synthesized from a logical theory), such as highly-optimized and
well-tested convolutional network architectures for image recognition [33]. In
such cases, the domain theory can refer to the interfaces of such components
(e.g., detectable features) without referring to their internal structure. Another
application of an explicit representation of the domain theory and its modular
structure might lie in meta-learning [27], sometimes referred to as a form of
automated machine learning , which could beneﬁt from richer representations
to learn abstract models about the hyper-parameters and performance of more
concrete models.
Towards a General Neuro-Symbolic Architecture. Machine learning and sym-
bolic reasoning technologies have been evolving rapidly in the last decade, albeit
mostly independently and driven by very di ↵erent technologies. Deep learning
architectures have been enabled by new, modular approaches to training large
neural networks, and they are simultaneously exploiting the explicit representa-
tion of dataﬂows for e �cient mappings into specialized, highly parallel hardware
and reﬂective metalevel algorithms (e.g., automatic di ↵erentiation). Symbolic
reasoning engines like theorem provers and SAT/SMT solvers, on the other
hand, can now perform millions of inferences per second or deal with problems
involving millions of variables, often enabled by highly optimized data structures
and algorithms that make e �cient use of general-purpose CPU architectures.
With its dual approximate and classical semantics, PALO o ↵ers a possible
semantic foundation for the synergistic integration of these emerging technolo-
gies. In our current PALO/LIME prototype, we combine symbolic and neural
computations in a stratiﬁed fashion, but apart from utilizing more general au-
tomated deduction capabilities as they have been explored in many applications
of Maude [12] and symbolic solvers such as Yices [65] that have been integrated
into Maude, we are also looking one step further into the future. Speciﬁcally, we
envision a neuro-symbolic architecture that supports dataﬂows in which approx-
imate computational inference and exact symbolic inference can take place in a
loosely coupled fashion with bidirectional knowledge transfer between symbolic
and neural forms of representation. We think a loose coupling, most suitably
in the form of a distributed and scalable networked implementation, is essential
to maintain the high e �ciencies of the participating technologies. In such a
framework, key research questions will be concerned with the types of knowl-
edge transfers and the distributed execution strategy. Ideally, a well-designed
general-purpose architecture should support multiple workﬂows including auto-
mated ones such as model learning with subsequent validation as well as interac-
tive workﬂows, e.g., knowledge engineering and model discovery with interactive
theory reﬁnement.

6. Conclusion
In Probabilistic Approximate Logic (PALO), which is heavily based on re-
cent advances in machine learning and neural networks, data and knowledge
are treated on an equal footing. Both are incorporated uniformly using axioms
of the underlying theory and usually exhibit uncertainly that can be approxi-
mately and probabilistically quantiﬁed. A theory is speciﬁed by a ﬁnite (often
incomplete) set of relevant quantiﬁable axioms that are expected properties of
our model. Such axioms might also be considered direct observables of our
models, and the role of our Logical Imagination Engine (LIME) is to synthesize
models only based on these directly observable properties. Although a better
understanding of the approximate inference process would be valuable, through
an independent validation we can assure not only that these axioms hold and to
what degree, but also validate and quantify any potentially implied properties.
We may also identify models with unexpected properties that may lead to new
discoveries, hypotheses, and reﬁned theories in the larger context of an iterative
knowledge engineering and model synthesis/validation process.
More generally, the role of a logical theory is that of a domain-speciﬁc reg-
ularizer for the set of models, which can partly compensate for a lower amount
or quality of data, and which can constrain the underlying neural networks to
maintain a whole range of properties with corresponding tradeo ↵s. Quite dif-
ferent from traditional symbolic inference systems or even model checkers, most
computational resources are spent on the synthesis of models (this is where the
use of highly parallel hardware such as GPUs is essential), as opposed to the
validation of their properties. The validation can be highly e �cient (even with-
out GPUs), which means that we can think of a model as a highly compressed
joint representation of theory and data in a form that can be e �ciently queried,
potentially leading to new logical applications, e.g., on mobile devices.
We would also like to recall from our earlier discussion that there is a com-
plementary viewpoint to the role of PALO as a language for knowledge repre-
sentation. We may equally think of it as the core of an architectural description
language for machine learning architectures. From a structural point of view,
a logical theory formalizes how black- or white-box components are combined
to achieve an overall performance objective (measured in terms of the observ-
able properties). This view provides an alternative motivation for several of our
proposed extensions, for example, the emphasis on equational logic to express
symmetries that can be directly realized by suitable architectural families. This
is very much in analogy to theories that are architecturally built into symbolic
engines such as Maude [64] and Yices [65], so that reasoning modulo such theo-
ries becomes highly e �cient. Composability and modularity are other desirable
features of both, knowledge representations and architectural speciﬁcations, and
hence important areas for future work.
In this paper, we have focused on the use of logic as a systematic means
of incorporating domain knowledge into machine learning to address a key con-
ceptual and engineering roadblock that is becoming increasingly important with
the growing diversity of deep learning applications. While we have used a simple
49

toy example in this paper to illustrate the concept, we also brieﬂy discussed our
experience with PALO/LIME and more complex domain theories, for example,
a theory of causal relations [62] that we applied to real-world settings, namely
in systems biology and in global ﬁnancial markets. Further increasing the com-
plexity of domain theories will be the primary objective of future extensions and
case studies.
There are other critical limitations of deep learning architectures, where a
logic-based approach can lead to improvements. For example, our approach
reduces the need for large annotated training sets by placing domain knowl-
edge on the same footing as and using it as a substitute for empirical data
(supporting semi-supervised, weakly supervised, and even unsupervised learn-
ing as illustrated by our toy application). A more general equational extension
of PALO (with structural equations) can directly be used to express feature
space symmetries, which can further reduce the amount of training data. The
limitation of current approaches that at best can only perform shallow infer-
ence is only partly addressed by the current version of PALO/LIME and would
be more completely addressed by a more general neuro-symbolic architecture
that can concurrently operate on neural representations optimized for (deep)
learning and symbolic representations that can enable (deep) inference.
Finally, it should be noted that we are concerned with an increasing range
of vulnerabilities of deep learning systems, e.g., safety concerns highlighted by
adversarial examples or privacy issues caused by learned representations that
are too informative. While partial generic solutions exist, it is unlikely that
such problems can be fully solved in a way that is completely agnostic to the
application and the system context, hence domain knowledge, logical structure,
inference, and a generalized notion of validation, can be expected to play a more
important role in these areas as well.
